pillar: Accessing RFA Treatment in China or India Through CancerFax

items.q: What is radiofrequency ablation, and which cancers is it used for?
items.a: Radiofrequency ablation, or RFA, uses a needle-like probe and heat from radio waves to destroy a tumour from the inside without open surgery. It is used most often for small liver tumours, and also for kidney, lung, bone and thyroid tumours. Doctors guide the probe using ultrasound or CT scanning. Whether RFA suits your tumour depends on its size, position, number of lesions and your overall health.

items.q: Is my tumour too large for RFA?
items.a: RFA works best for tumours up to about three centimetres, and may still be considered up to five centimetres in selected patients. Larger tumours are harder to destroy completely in one session, so doctors may combine RFA with chemoembolisation or choose surgery instead. Position matters as much as size, because tumours near large blood vessels, the bile duct or the bowel carry extra risk. Only the treating team can confirm suitability after reviewing your scans.

items.q: How much does RFA cost in India and China?
items.a: RFA typically costs about USD 3,000 to 6,000 in India and roughly USD 4,000 to 8,000 in China, including the procedure, a short hospital stay and imaging. Prices rise if you need several sessions, general anaesthesia, or RFA combined with chemoembolisation. These are estimates only. Your final bill depends on the hospital, the diagnostics you need on arrival, any complications, and how long you stay.

items.q: Is RFA as good as surgery for a small liver tumour?
items.a: For single liver tumours under three centimetres, RFA can give survival results close to surgical removal, with a shorter recovery and less blood loss. Surgery still tends to control larger tumours better, and gives a clearer picture of the tumour margin. The right choice depends on tumour size and site, liver function, cirrhosis, and whether a transplant is planned. Your hepatobiliary team should weigh these before deciding.

items.q: How is RFA done, and will I be awake?
items.a: RFA is usually done through a small skin puncture under sedation or general anaesthesia, so you feel little or nothing during it. The doctor guides a thin probe into the tumour using ultrasound or CT, then heats the tip for about ten to twenty minutes to destroy the tissue. Most people go home within one to two days. Some centres perform RFA during keyhole or open surgery instead.

items.q: How long will I need to stay in India or China for RFA?
items.a: Plan for roughly two to three weeks abroad for a single RFA session. Expect a few days for consultation and fresh scans, one to two nights in hospital around the procedure, then about a week before a follow-up scan confirms the tumour was fully destroyed. If a second session is needed, or if you develop fever or pain, the stay can be longer, so keep your return flight flexible.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of RFA?
items.a: Most people get mild pain, low fever and tiredness for a few days, known as post-ablation syndrome. Serious problems are uncommon but real: bleeding, infection or abscess, injury to the bile duct, bowel or diaphragm, and a collapsed lung when lung tumours are treated. Rarely, tumour cells can spread along the needle track. Ask your interventional radiologist about the risks in your case.

items.q: Which hospitals in India and China offer RFA?
items.a: Large cancer and liver centres in both countries offer RFA, including Tata Memorial and major private hospitals in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Bengaluru, and specialist liver hospitals in Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou. What matters more than the name is how many ablations the interventional radiology team performs each year and whether they have the imaging to guide difficult tumours. Availability and acceptance vary, so confirm both before booking travel.

items.q: What medical records do I need to send before a hospital will accept me for RFA?
items.a: Send a recent CT or MRI scan with the actual images, not just the report, plus your biopsy or pathology report, tumour marker results, liver and kidney function tests, and a summary of treatment so far. CancerFax passes this package to interventional radiology teams in India and China and returns their written opinion and cost estimate. Old or low-quality imaging is the most common reason a case is sent back.

items.q: How do I start the process, and what happens after RFA?
items.a: Start by having your scans reviewed, because no hospital will confirm RFA or quote a price without seeing the images. After the procedure you need a scan at about one month, then every three to six months, since tumours can come back at the edge of the treated area and may be ablated again. CancerFax can help arrange the review, medical visa and follow-up, alongside the oncologist who should confirm the plan suits you.
